newsitem.title: UNITED NATIONS: China urges sharing of development technology.
newsitem.headline: China urges sharing of development technology.

text.p: China said on Monday developed countries had a historical responsibility to share new science and technology on the environment and development with the Third World.
State Councillor Song Jian was addressing a 173-nation conference reviewing progress on protecting the environment since the 1992 Earth Summit in Rio de Janeiro.

Song, whose rank is comparable to that of a deputy prime minister, said: "Science and technology, as the common wealth of mankind, are the very foundation of the improvement of their patterns of production and consumption and the achievement of sustainable development."

The international community should make joint efforts to expand the development and application of science and technology in these areas "through flexible and diversified ways of cooperation," he said.

"Developed countries have the capability and unshirkable historical responsibility to share with developing countries the achievements of a new round of scientific and technological revolution," he continued.

"The protection of intellectual property rights should become a booster for the advancement and popularisation of science and technology, instead of barriers hindering science and technology from serving mankind as a whole," added Song, whose country has sometimes clashed with the United States over such property rights issues as the unlicensed production of compact discs.

He also called for an end to various kinds of trade protectionism, the establishment of an "equitable, rational and integrated multilateral trading system" and measures to reverse the "trend of sharp decrease in development funding for developing countries."
While developing countries should actively seek international support and assistance, they should "fully tap their own potentials."

"They cannot and should not follow the same old development patterns of developed countries in 'pollution first and treatment later,' but rather take the road of sustainable development right from the initial stage of development."

Song said China, the world's biggest developing country with one-fifth of the global population, had registered rapid economic growth in recent years while basically avoiding drastic environment degradation and even registering some partial improvement.

Acknowledging that it still faced severe challenges in achieving sustainable development, he said China would "contribute significantly to global environmental protection and economic development by running her own affairs well."
